Now consider the curiosity/practical‐experience disjunction: ‘Either Noel is curious or Noel has practical experience, but not both.’ Since he lacks practical experience, the first part must be true: Noel is curious. Moreover, it says they are not both, so we still have Noel = curious and Noel ≠ has_practical_experience.

Next, look at the conditional: ‘If either Noel has a good memory or Noel is curious, but not both, then Noel is innovative.’

Moreover, if he had a good memory, the antecedent of that implication collapses to false, so there is no entailment of innovation either.

Therefore nothing forces ‘has a good memory’ to be true. But the question is asking whether the context ENTAILS the conclusion. Entailment means it must be true in every model that satisfies the context. Here we can have a consistent model with Noel lacking a good memory (and hence being innovative) or one with Noel having a good memory (then the conditional’s antecedent fails, so he might or might not be innovative, but nothing breaks). In both cases the rest of the statements can be satisfied. So ‘Noel has a good memory’ is neither entailed nor contradicted: its truth is not determined by the context.
